body:
Two systems of government in colonial Gujarat

Before Indian independence in 1947, the territory of present-day Gujarat was not governed by a single administration. Some areas, including Ahmedabad and Kheda, were administered directly by the British government as parts of British India. Other areas were ruled by Indian princes under British paramountcy.

The princely states were particularly numerous in Kathiawar, now commonly called Saurashtra. Important princely centres included Rajkot, Bhavnagar, Junagadh, Gondal and Nawanagar. Baroda was another major princely state. The rulers of these states controlled many internal administrative matters, but their authority operated under British supremacy.

British paramountcy

Paramountcy was the superior authority exercised by the British Crown over Indian princely states. A prince could exercise internal powers, but the state was not fully sovereign or independent of British control.

This distinction matters because the political demands of the people differed according to the system under which they lived. Nationalists in British-administered areas challenged colonial government directly. People in princely states often challenged the arbitrary exercise of power by rulers and their officials while also questioning British protection of the princely order.

Why Praja Mandal movements developed

In many princely states, political power was concentrated in the ruler, the diwan and appointed officials. Ordinary subjects had little effective control over taxation, expenditure or administration. Freedom of speech, publication, association and public assembly could be restricted. Some states established representative bodies, but these often lacked the power to make the government answerable to the people.

Educated residents, lawyers, journalists, merchants, social workers and, increasingly, peasants began organising to raise public grievances. These organisations were commonly known as Praja Mandals, Praja Parishads or political conferences. The terms varied between regions, but their central purpose was to organise the subjects of princely states and demand political rights.

Responsible government

A responsible government is one in which ministers and the executive are answerable to representatives of the people. It involves more than appointing advisers or allowing a limited assembly to submit recommendations that the ruler may reject.

Principal democratic demands

The demands developed over time, but several appeared repeatedly in princely-state movements:

  • Civil liberties: Freedom of speech, press, public meetings and political association.
  • Representative institutions: Assemblies with an increasing proportion of elected members.
  • Responsible administration: Ministers answerable to representatives rather than solely to the ruler.
  • Financial accountability: Reduction of arbitrary taxes, restrictions on excessive expenditure and greater attention to public services.
  • Fair treatment: Relief from administrative oppression, recognition of public organisations and release of political prisoners.

Early organisations often submitted petitions and sought reforms without demanding the immediate abolition of princely rule. As political mobilisation expanded during the 1930s and 1940s, demands became stronger and public protests more common.

A princely state was not a directly governed British province. Equally, an advisory assembly established by a prince did not necessarily constitute responsible government. The decisive issue was whether the people could exercise effective control over administration.

Prelims focus

  • British-administered provinces and princely states were distinct political units before 1947.
  • British paramountcy limited the independence of princely rulers.
  • Praja Mandals and Praja Parishads organised political demands within princely states.
  • Responsible government required executive accountability to representatives of the people.
  • Civil liberties, elected representation and financial accountability were major demands.
  • Trap: A ruler's advisory council was not necessarily a democratic legislature.

[NCERT, Politics in India Since Independence, Class 12, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 14–16; IGNOU, MHI-09, Unit 19, Political Democratisation in the Princely States, printed pp. 51–54, sections 19.3–19.5, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Residents in 1920s Kathiawar gather on woven mats in a modest hall as a local organiser addresses their grievances.
pictures.caption: Public discussion and petitions became early methods of political mobilisation in princely Gujarat.

pictures.alt: Ruler control and advisory representation differ from responsible government, where ministers and the executive answer to elected representatives.
pictures.caption: The central constitutional distinction was between the ruler's authority and accountability to the people.

title: Princely Gujarat and the Rise of Demands for Responsible Government

body:
Why regional political organisations were necessary

Kathiawar contained many princely states with separate rulers and administrations. Political activists therefore faced a practical difficulty: people could share similar problems but remain divided by state boundaries. A regional political conference allowed them to discuss common issues, exchange information and develop coordinated demands.

The Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad, also called the Kathiawar Political Conference, emerged in 1921. Its first meeting took place at Rajkot. Vithalbhai Patel was associated with its early leadership, while activists including Mansukhlal Mehta and Amritlal Sheth helped develop political organisation in the region.

The Parishad was not a government of Kathiawar. It was a political forum for subjects and public workers seeking reform within the princely states. Its work helped connect local complaints about taxes and administration with the larger demand for public participation in government.

Representative bodies established by rulers

Some rulers introduced limited institutions of representation. These reforms are important because they show both the spread of political ideas and the difference between consultation and democracy.

StateInstitutional developmentYearImportant limitation
BarodaRepresentative assembly1907Representation did not establish full executive accountability.
RajkotPraja Pratinidhi Sabha under Lakhajiraj1923The body could make recommendations; decisive authority remained with the ruler.

The Praja Pratinidhi Sabha in Rajkot was an institution established under the ruler. It should not be confused with the Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad, which was a regional political organisation. Their names both refer to public representation, but their constitutional positions were different.

All-India coordination in 1927

Political consciousness was increasing in princely states throughout India. To coordinate these movements, the All-India States' Peoples' Conference, commonly abbreviated as AISPC, was established in Bombay in December 1927. Representatives of 70 states attended its first meeting.

The AISPC provided a common platform for political organisations functioning in different princely states. It expressed their democratic demands and helped bring the questions of civil liberties and responsible government into the wider Indian national movement.

Relationship with the Indian National Congress

The Indian National Congress and the princely-state organisations shared the broader objective of political freedom, but they were not identical bodies. Congress initially maintained a cautious position towards direct intervention in the internal politics of princely states. Local organisations therefore carried much of the responsibility for initiating and sustaining these movements.

As popular movements intensified, Congress support became more explicit. At the Haripura session in 1938, the Congress recognised the relevance of its independence objective to princely-state populations while maintaining that their immediate struggles should be conducted through their own organisations. Its engagement with princely-state movements increased in the following period.

Among the prominent political workers associated with the region were Balwantrai Mehta, who played an important role in the wider states' peoples' movement, and Uchchhrangrai Navalshankar Dhebar, commonly known as U. N. Dhebar, who became a leading figure in the Rajkot struggle.

Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad: Regional political coordination in Kathiawar, beginning in 1921. AISPC: All-India coordination of princely-state peoples' organisations, beginning in 1927. Neither was the same as a ruler's advisory assembly.

Prelims focus

  • Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad: first meeting at Rajkot in 1921.
  • Baroda had a representative assembly from 1907.
  • Rajkot's Praja Pratinidhi Sabha was established under Lakhajiraj in 1923.
  • AISPC was established at Bombay in December 1927.
  • The first AISPC meeting represented 70 princely states.
  • Trap: The Kathiawar Political Conference of 1921 and the all-India conference of 1927 were different organisations.

[IGNOU, MHI-09, Unit 19, Political Democratisation in the Princely States, printed pp. 53–55, sections 19.4–19.5, consulted 22 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Rajkot District, History of Rajkot, entries for 1921 and 1923, consulted 22 November 2026; Prime Ministers Museum and Library, Institutional Collections, All-India States' Peoples' Conference, introductory history, consulted 22 November 2026; Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 28, The Freedom Struggle in Princely India.]

pictures.alt: Local groups connect with the Kathiawar regional movement and wider all-India coordination through political platforms, not governments.
pictures.caption: Local and regional organisations could coordinate through a common all-India platform.

title: Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad, Local Organisations and the All-India States' Peoples' Conference

body:
Background: dissatisfaction with Rajkot's administration

The Rajkot Satyagraha was one of the most important princely-state movements in Gujarat. It developed from local opposition to the arbitrary exercise of power and grew into a struggle over responsible government.

Under Thakore Sahib Dharmendrasinhji, public dissatisfaction increased over taxation, government expenditure, commercial monopolies granted by the state and the weakening of effective public consultation. The role of the ruler's adviser, Dewan Virawala, also became a focus of criticism.

A state monopoly meant that the administration granted exclusive control over a particular activity or commodity. Such arrangements could raise prices and restrict ordinary economic activity. The Rajkot agitation therefore combined everyday economic grievances with the demand that the ruler's government answer to the people.

Local mobilisation before the main satyagraha

Political resistance did not begin suddenly with Mahatma Gandhi's intervention in 1939. Local activists had already spent years organising people.

In 1936, Gandhian worker Jethalal Joshi organised workers at a state-owned cotton mill and led a strike for improved working conditions. This encouraged confidence in collective action.

In March 1937, activists including Joshi and U. N. Dhebar helped revive the Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad's activities. The demand for responsible government was accompanied by demands to reduce taxation and state expenditure.

In August 1938, opposition to a gambling monopoly at a local fair led to protests and police action. Public discontent increased. Dhebar and other workers organised continued resistance, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel took up the demand for constitutional reform.

The settlement and its breakdown

In December 1938, negotiations involving Sardar Patel produced an agreement under which a committee was to consider constitutional reforms in Rajkot. The arrangement provided for public representatives to be recommended by Patel alongside members appointed by the state.

A dispute arose when the ruler did not implement the agreed arrangement as Patel and the movement's leaders understood it. For the protesters, the issue was no longer only the original economic grievances; it was also whether a public promise of reform would be honoured.

Kasturba Gandhi joined the struggle and was arrested in Rajkot on 2 February 1939. Maniben Patel also participated in the movement.

Gandhi's fast and arbitration in 1939

Mahatma Gandhi intervened personally after the dispute over the reform agreement remained unresolved. He began a fast at Rajkot on 3 March 1939 to protest the breach of trust. He ended the fast on 7 March 1939 after a proposal to submit the dispute for arbitration.

Sir Maurice Gwyer, the Chief Justice of the Federal Court, was appointed as arbitrator. On 3 April 1939, his award supported the claim advanced by the people's representatives regarding the settlement.

However, this was not the immediate establishment of fully responsible government in Rajkot. The subsequent implementation of reform remained disputed, and Gandhi later decided not to insist on the award as the basis of settlement. The movement is therefore best understood as an important struggle for democratic accountability rather than a simple story of an instant constitutional victory.

Why the movement matters

The Rajkot struggle showed how the national movement and princely-state politics could interact. Dhebar and local workers developed public organisation; Patel negotiated political reforms; Kasturba Gandhi and Maniben Patel participated in resistance; and Mahatma Gandhi intervened when the settlement broke down.

It also demonstrated that satyagraha could be directed against an Indian princely administration, not only against directly governed British territory.

Prelims focus

  • Rajkot Satyagraha was a princely-state movement for administrative reform and responsible government.
  • U. N. Dhebar was a major local organiser.
  • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel negotiated a reform settlement in December 1938.
  • Kasturba Gandhi was arrested at Rajkot on 2 February 1939.
  • Gandhi's Rajkot fast lasted from 3 to 7 March 1939.
  • Sir Maurice Gwyer's arbitration award was delivered on 3 April 1939.
  • Trap: The arbitration award did not mean that full responsible government was immediately established.

[Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 28, The Freedom Struggle in Princely India, section on Rajkot; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology of Mahatma Gandhi, entries for 2 February, 3 March, 7 March and 16 April 1939, consulted 22 November 2026; The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Volumes 68–69, introductory summaries of the Rajkot struggle, National Digital Library of India, consulted 22 November 2026; The Indian Express, account of the Rajkot Satyagraha and Rashtriya Shala, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The Rajkot agitation connected local economic grievances with the demand for political rights.
